Stay active and maintain regular mealtimes to give your marrow steady building materials. If you supplement, avoid oversized doses unless recommended for you. Use RDW‑SD as a helpful companion to other blood count markers, not as a stand‑alone answer.

name: Reticulocytes abs.
description:
Reticulocytes are very young red blood cells that have just left the bone marrow and are maturing in the bloodstream. An absolute reticulocyte count tells you the actual number of these cells in a set volume of blood. It shows how actively your bone marrow is making new red cells at the moment. This information complements hemoglobin and other red cell indices to give a fuller picture of red blood cell health. Small day‑to‑day differences are common, so patterns across time are most informative.
A higher reticulocyte count can occur after blood loss, when red cells are being broken down faster than usual, or when treatment for a deficiency is starting to work. A lower count may be seen when the marrow is not getting the building blocks it needs, such as iron, vitamin B12, or folate. It can also be lower with some chronic conditions, kidney issues that reduce erythropoietin, or certain medications. Altitude, pregnancy, and lab methods can influence results, so context is important. By itself the reticulocyte count does not diagnose the cause, but it helps point to whether production is brisk or slow.
You can support healthy red cell production by getting adequate iron, B12, folate, and protein through a varied diet. If you follow a vegetarian or vegan pattern, consider fortified foods or supplements for B12 after discussing with your clinician. Moderate alcohol intake and attentive management of chronic conditions help protect the marrow’s ability to make cells. Stay up to date with routine checkups if you are on medications that can affect blood counts. If your numbers change a lot or you feel unwell, seek personalized guidance rather than self‑treating.

name: Reticulocytes %
description:
Reticulocytes are young red blood cells that still contain bits of RNA. Reticulocytes % tells you what portion of your red cells are newly released from the bone marrow. It reflects how strongly your marrow is making red cells at the time of the test. Automated analyzers detect these cells with special dyes and counting methods. The result is commonly used to provide context when evaluating anemia or recovery.

A higher percentage suggests increased production, which can happen after blood loss, during recovery from iron, B12, or folate deficiency, or when red cells are being broken down faster. A lower percentage suggests reduced production and can occur with nutrient shortages, chronic illness, or marrow suppression. Because the value is a percentage, it can look higher when total red cells are low and lower when total red cells are high. Trends over time and related tests, like hemoglobin and iron studies, are important for interpretation. By itself, the percentage does not diagnose a condition.

Support healthy red cell production by getting enough iron, B12, and folate from foods or clinician guided supplements when needed. If you have heavy menstrual bleeding or donate blood frequently, talk with a clinician about iron needs and timing of tests. A diet rich in legumes, leafy greens, lean proteins, and vitamin C containing foods helps the body make hemoglobin. Limit heavy alcohol use and prioritize sleep, as these factors affect marrow function. Share persistent changes with a clinician so your whole picture can be reviewed.

name: Reverse T3 (rT3)
description:
Reverse T3 is an inactive form of thyroid hormone made when the body converts T4 in a way that blocks activity. The body naturally makes some rT3, and levels can rise during illness, fasting, or major stress as an energy‑saving response. rT3 does not activate thyroid receptors like T3 does. For most people, it is not needed for routine thyroid evaluation. When measured, it should be viewed alongside TSH, free T4, free T3, and your clinical picture.
Higher rT3 may be seen with severe illness, calorie restriction, trauma, or certain medicines, and it often moves back toward baseline during recovery. A low rT3 is rarely meaningful by itself and may reflect lab variation. High‑dose biotin and some supplements can interfere with certain immunoassays and skew results. Professional societies do not recommend using rT3 to diagnose hypothyroidism. Decisions rely on symptoms and standard thyroid tests rather than this value alone.
Support thyroid health by eating enough calories and protein and by including iodine, selenium, and iron from foods without megadosing. Manage stress and prioritize sleep to normalize hormone signaling. Do not start or stop thyroid medicines without medical advice. If you take biotin, follow lab instructions about pausing it before testing to avoid assay interference. Share results and symptoms with a clinician for full‑context interpretation.

name: SCC antigen (squamous cell carcinoma antigen)
description:
SCC antigen (squamous cell carcinoma antigen) is a protein that can be released by certain squamous cells. In specialty care, it may be used to monitor some cancers over time, but it is not a screening tool and cannot diagnose cancer by itself. Levels can also rise with non‑cancerous skin, lung, or liver conditions. Lab methods vary and results can differ between centers. For wellness use, SCC antigen should be considered a highly specialized marker requiring expert context.
Higher SCC antigen can have many explanations unrelated to cancer, and small shifts can be due to measurement variation. Lower or stable values are common and not necessarily meaningful on their own. Because so many factors can influence this marker, a one‑time result is rarely informative. Interpretation belongs with a clinician who knows the full picture, including symptoms and imaging when relevant. Using the same lab for follow‑up can make trends easier to understand.
While SCC antigen is not a general wellness test, broad habits still support skin and overall health. Protect your skin from excessive sun, avoid smoking, and keep alcohol modest. Eat a colorful, fiber‑rich diet and stay active to support immune balance and healing. Prioritize sleep and stress management, which influence many body systems. Keep up with routine, evidence‑based screenings appropriate for your age and risk rather than relying on tumor markers.

name: Selenium
description:
Selenium is a trace mineral that plays a critical role in the body, primarily as a component of antioxidant enzymes. These enzymes protect cells from damage by free radicals, which are harmful compounds that can contribute to chronic diseases. Selenium is also essential for the proper functioning of the immune system and thyroid gland, influencing metabolism and overall health. Additionally, it supports reproductive health, DNA synthesis, and helps prevent cell damage.

Selenium deficiency can lead to several health issues. One of the most notable is Keshan disease, a potentially fatal form of heart disease linked to low selenium levels. Selenium deficiency can also contribute to Kashin-Beck disease, a type of osteoarthropathy. Other potential effects of low selenium include weakened immune response, making the body more susceptible to illness, and hypothyroidism, as selenium is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones.

Selenium toxicity, known as selenosis, can occur from excessive intake, often due to over-supplementation. Symptoms of selenium toxicity include hair and nail loss or brittleness, skin rashes, nausea, fatigue, irritability, and nervous system abnormalities. In severe cases, it can lead to problems with the nervous system, heart, and liver.

Selenium and iodine work closely in thyroid function. Selenium is a component of enzymes that help convert thyroid hormones into their active form. While selenium doesn't directly interfere with iodine absorption, a deficiency in selenium can exacerbate the effects of iodine deficiency on thyroid health, and vice versa.

To maintain healthy blood selenium levels:


Ensure an adequate intake of selenium through a balanced diet that includes foods such as Brazil nuts, seafood, poultry, eggs, and whole grains.
If you have a thyroid condition, work closely with your healthcare provider to monitor your selenium levels and ensure they are in balance with your iodine levels for optimal thyroid function.
​​​

name: Serum osmolality
description:
Serum osmolality is a direct measurement of how concentrated your blood is, based on how water freezes in the sample. It reflects the total number of dissolved particles that pull water across cell membranes. Common contributors include sodium, glucose, and urea, but many substances can play a role. Because it is measured directly, it can reveal changes not captured by formulas. It is a core snapshot of water balance and solute load at the time of testing.
Higher serum osmolality indicates a more concentrated blood fluid and can be seen with dehydration or higher sodium or glucose. Lower values indicate a more dilute fluid and can happen with overhydration or lower sodium states. Differences between measured and calculated osmolality can hint at unmeasured substances, lab variation, or timing. A single value is not diagnostic and should be interpreted with electrolytes, glucose, and your hydration story. Testing conditions, like recent exercise or large drinks, can shift results temporarily.
To support steady osmolality, hydrate regularly, adjusting for weather and activity, and include electrolytes during long, sweaty sessions. Keep sugary drinks modest and build balanced meals that help stabilize glucose. Aim for consistent sleep and stress management, which influence thirst and hormone signals. If you use diuretics or other medications that affect fluids, follow guidance closely and keep your routine predictable. When comparing results, try to match fasting status, activity, and fluid intake so you are comparing like with like.

name: SHBG
description:
Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin (SHBG) is a protein produced by the liver, playing a critical role in regulating the levels of sex hormones, particularly testosterone and estrogen, in the blood. SHBG binds to these hormones, effectively controlling the amount of testosterone and estrogen that is free or active in the bloodstream. This binding action is vital because only unbound or ""free"" hormones can be biologically active and exert effects in the body. SHBG levels are used to understand the balance and bioavailability of sex hormones, impacting various physiological processes and conditions.

Elevated SHBG levels can lead to a decrease in the bioavailability of sex hormones, particularly testosterone. In men, high SHBG can result in symptoms of low testosterone, such as reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased muscle mass, and fatigue, despite having normal total testosterone levels. In women, high SHBG might mask symptoms of high estrogen levels. Elevated SHBG can be caused by factors such as liver disease, hyperthyroidism, and certain medications.

Conversely, low SHBG levels can increase the bioavailability of sex hormones. In men, this might not cause symptoms unless it leads to an abnormality in testosterone levels. In women, low SHBG can contribute to symptoms associated with excessive free testosterone, such as in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), leading to irregular menstrual cycles, hirsutism (excess hair growth), and acne. Factors that can lower SHBG include obesity, hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes, and excessive growth hormone. Balancing SHBG levels involves addressing underlying health issues and managing lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise.​​​

name: Silicon
description:
Silicon is a naturally occurring trace element found in food, drinking water, and the environment. In the body it is present mostly as orthosilicic acid, a form that circulates in small amounts. Humans do not have an official recommended dietary allowance for silicon, and it is not classified as an essential nutrient. Research suggests it may contribute to normal connective tissue and bone formation, but evidence in people is still developing. A blood or urine test reflects recent exposure and intake rather than a stored reserve.
Higher silicon results are most often related to greater intake from beverages, supplements, or occupational exposure such as dust. People with reduced kidney function may clear silicon more slowly, which can make values appear higher. Lower values are usually not linked to a specific deficiency syndrome in humans. Because labs and sampling methods differ, small shifts from one test to the next can occur without a meaningful change in health. The measurement is best interpreted with your overall diet, workplace exposures, and kidney health in mind.
You can support a sensible intake by focusing on varied whole foods like oats, barley, whole‑grain breads, green beans, and mineral waters without chasing high doses. Avoid unproven high‑dose silicon supplements unless a clinician specifically recommends them. Use appropriate protective equipment and ventilation if you work around dust, concrete cutting, or ceramics. Stay hydrated so your kidneys can filter and excrete trace elements normally. Share persistent out‑of‑range results with a healthcare professional, who can place your number in context and decide whether any follow‑up is needed.

name: Sodium
description:
Sodium as a blood biomarker significantly influences several bodily functions. When maintained within its physiological range, sodium ensures proper nerve and muscle function, aids in maintaining fluid balance across cell membranes, and plays a vital role in the functioning of the heart and brain. It is also essential for the absorption and transport of certain nutrients and maintains the osmotic balance critical for cell health.

Hyponatremia, or low blood sodium, can result from various conditions like kidney disease, heart failure, or excessive fluid intake. This condition can lead to neurological symptoms such as headache, confusion, and fatigue, progressing to more severe complications like seizures, coma, and potentially life-threatening brain swelling. Hyponatremia affects cellular function and fluid balance, disrupting normal physiological processes.

Hypernatremia, or high blood sodium, often results from dehydration or excessive salt intake and can impair kidney function. This condition manifests as intense thirst, confusion, muscle weakness, and in severe cases, can cause neurological damage and is associated with a higher risk of mortality. Hypernatremia disrupts cellular homeostasis, leading to complications in various organ systems.

To maintain healthy blood sodium levels:


Stay hydrated by drinking adequate water throughout the day
Follow a balanced diet and be mindful of sodium intake, especially from processed and packaged foods
Be cautious with salt substitutes and supplements containing sodium
Manage underlying health conditions that may affect sodium levels, such as kidney disease or heart failure
​​​

name: Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR)
description:
Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) is a small piece of the iron‑transport doorway that cells shed into the blood. When cells demand more iron, they display more receptors, and a portion circulates as sTfR that can be measured. Because of that biology, sTfR gives a sense of the body’s iron need rather than the stored iron alone. It is less affected by inflammation than ferritin, although illness and growth can still influence it. Labs may use different assays and ranges, so it is best viewed together with ferritin, hemoglobin, and transferrin saturation.
Higher sTfR usually means cells are asking for more iron, which is common with low iron intake, rapid growth, pregnancy, or recovery from blood loss. It can also be raised when the bone marrow is very active making red cells, such as after high‑altitude exposure or in some anemias. Normal or low sTfR suggests iron demand is not especially high, but does not guarantee that iron stores are abundant. In inflammatory states, ferritin can look higher than it truly is, and sTfR can help balance the picture without being perfect. A single value is only a clue, and decisions about iron therapy should not be made from one number alone.
To support healthy iron balance, include foods like legumes, lean meats, seafood, fortified grains, nuts, and leafy greens in regular meals. Pair plant sources with vitamin C–rich foods to aid absorption, and avoid tea or coffee right with iron‑rich meals if you are working to raise iron. Athletes, frequent blood donors, and people with heavy periods may benefit from routine check‑ins because needs can change over time. Only use iron supplements under guidance, since too much iron can accumulate and cause problems. Remember that sTfR is an educational marker and must be interpreted by a clinician together with symptoms and other labs.

name: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG)
description:
TBG is a carrier protein made in the liver. Its job is to carry thyroid hormones (T4 and T3) in the bloodstream and keep a small, steady amount available to your cells. Because TBG binds most of the hormone, changes in TBG can make ""total"" hormone tests (TT4, TT3) look higher or lower—even when your thyroid itself is fine. What really tells how your thyroid is doing are TSH and the ""free"" hormones (FT4, FT3).
When TBG is low
If TBG is low, total T4/T3 often look low, but free T4/T3 and TSH are usually normal—so you may feel fine and not need treatment. Common reasons:

  Androgen (testosterone) therapy can lower TBG, sometimes lowering the LT4 dose needed in people on thyroid replacement.[Arafah, 1994]
  Protein loss (e.g., nephrotic syndrome) lowers TBG and total hormones; levels usually improve as the condition improves.[Afrasiabi, 1979]
  Severe illness (e.g., sepsis) can lower TBG and total T4 temporarily.[McIver & Gorman, 1997]

When TBG is high
If TBG is high, total T4/T3 often look high, but free T4/T3 and TSH stay normal once the body re‑balances. Common reasons:

  Pregnancy and estrogen therapy (e.g., birth‑control pills, HRT) raise TBG. If you take levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, you often need a dose increase when starting estrogen or during pregnancy. Consult this with your clinician.[Alexander, 2017][Arafah, 2001][Ain, 1987]
  Some liver diseases can increase binding proteins, including TBG.[Huang et al., 1989]

How to keep your thyroid tests accurate and easy to read

  Always check TSH and free hormones (FT4 ± FT3) alongside total T4/T3. That shows your true thyroid statuseven if TBG is high or low.[Koulouri, 2013][Bartalena & Robbins, 1992]
  Tell your clinician if you''re pregnant, starting estrogen, or using androgens (testosterone)—you might need a levothyroxine dose adjustment if you''re on thyroid medication.[Alexander, 2017][Arafah, 2001][Arafah, 1994]
  If you''ve had kidney protein loss or a serious infection, your totals may be off for a while—recheck once you''ve recovered.[Afrasiabi, 1979]

name: Thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg Ab / ATG)
description:
Thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg Ab) are immune proteins that attach to thyroglobulin, a normal protein made by your thyroid gland. This test looks for those antibodies in your blood. Clinicians use it to understand whether the immune system is reacting to thyroid tissue. Tg antibodies can also affect thyroglobulin measurements, which are sometimes used to follow certain thyroid conditions. The result adds context to other thyroid tests rather than standing on its own.

Higher Tg Ab levels suggest immune activity around the thyroid, which is common in autoimmune thyroid conditions. Some people without thyroid symptoms can also have detectable antibodies, and values can fluctuate over time. A lower or negative result does not rule out thyroid problems, and a higher result does not prove one either. Because antibodies can bind to thyroglobulin, they may make thyroglobulin blood tests read lower or harder to interpret. Results are usually considered together with TSH, T4, symptoms, imaging, and clinical history.

To support thyroid wellness, aim for steady iodine intake from regular food sources such as iodized salt, dairy, and seafood rather than large sporadic supplements. A balanced diet with adequate selenium, zinc, and iron supports normal thyroid hormone pathways, but supplements should be guided by a clinician. Manage stress, sleep well, and avoid smoking, as these habits support overall immune balance. If you take biotin, high doses can interfere with some thyroid assays, so follow your lab instructions about pausing it before testing. Share your results with your healthcare professional if you have symptoms like fatigue, temperature sensitivity, or neck swelling, since the right next step depends on the whole picture.

name: TIBC
description:
Total iron‑binding capacity (TIBC) estimates how much iron your blood proteins, mainly transferrin, could carry if fully loaded. It is part of an iron panel that often includes serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation. TIBC rises when the body makes more transferrin to capture scarce iron, and falls when less transferrin is produced. Results may be given directly or calculated from transferrin concentration. Because it reflects transport capacity, TIBC complements storage markers like ferritin.
A higher TIBC is commonly seen when iron stores are low or during pregnancy, when transferrin production naturally increases. A lower TIBC can appear with inflammation, chronic illness, malnutrition, or liver disease that reduces protein production. Dehydration and sample timing can cause small shifts from day to day. Different laboratories may use different calculation factors, leading to modest method differences. The result is not diagnostic by itself and is best read with ferritin, transferrin saturation, and your symptoms.
Support iron balance with foods like legumes, leafy greens, fortified grains, eggs, and lean meats if you eat them. Combine iron‑containing foods with vitamin C sources such as citrus, tomatoes, or peppers to aid absorption. Avoid starting iron supplements on your own, since too much iron can be harmful. Athletes, frequent blood donors, and those with heavy periods may benefit from periodic evaluation with a clinician. When tracking changes, use the same lab and similar timing to improve comparability.

name: Total Cholesterol
description:
Cholesterol, a waxy, fat-like substance found in all cells of the body, is essential for producing cell membranes, certain hormones, and vitamin D. It's also important for the formation of bile acids, which help in the digestion of fats. The body produces all the cholesterol it needs, but it also obtains cholesterol from food. Total cholesterol in the blood is a combination of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and triglycerides.

High total cholesterol levels can increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases, such as heart disease and stroke. This is primarily due to the build-up of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which can lead to the formation of plaque in the arteries (atherosclerosis). Plaque narrows and hardens the arteries, limiting blood flow and potentially causing blood clots that can lead to a heart attack or stroke. Elevated cholesterol can be due to genetic factors, an unhealthy diet, obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, and certain medical conditions or medications.

Low total cholesterol levels are generally not a concern and are often seen as beneficial in reducing the risk of heart disease. However, extremely low cholesterol levels, though rare, might be a sign of an underlying health issue, such as hyperthyroidism, malnutrition, or liver disease. Maintaining a balanced cholesterol level is important, and it's usually managed through diet, lifestyle changes, and, if necessary, medication. The focus is often on reducing high LDL ("bad") cholesterol and increasing HDL ("good") cholesterol levels to improve the overall cholesterol profile.

To maintain healthy total cholesterol levels:


Adopt a heart-healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats while limiting saturated and trans fats, as well as dietary cholesterol.
Engage in regular physical activity, as exercise can help raise HDL ("good") cholesterol levels and improve overall cardiovascular health[Franczyk, 2023].
Maintain a healthy weight, as obesity can contribute to elevated cholesterol levels and increase the risk of related health problems.
If you have a family history of high cholesterol or are at increased risk, work with your healthcare provider to monitor your cholesterol levels regularly and develop a personalized management plan.
​​​

name: Total Cholesterol/HDL ratio
description:
The total cholesterol/HDL ratio compares all measured cholesterol to the fraction carried by HDL. A lower ratio generally indicates a more favorable lipid pattern. It is a simple summary number that some clinicians use to estimate risk. However, it does not show particle number or the role of triglycerides. Non‑HDL cholesterol and ApoB can add important detail.
The ratio changes with diet, exercise, weight, genetics, and medications. Because total cholesterol includes HDL itself, changes in HDL also move the ratio. One result does not diagnose disease, and small lab‑to‑lab differences can occur. Looking at trends and the rest of the lipid panel gives a clearer picture. Your personal risk also depends on blood pressure, glucose, smoking, and family history.
Improve the ratio by lowering LDL and triglycerides and by supporting HDL with regular activity. Choose a plant‑forward, fiber‑rich pattern with healthy fats and fewer refined carbohydrates. Maintain a healthy waist size and avoid tobacco. Work with a clinician to select targets that match your risk and to consider ApoB or non‑HDL as primary guides. Recheck after lifestyle or therapy changes to track progress.

name: Total Protein
description:
Total protein adds together the major proteins in your blood, mainly albumin and globulins. Albumin helps keep fluid in the bloodstream and carries hormones and medicines. Globulins include antibodies and other transport proteins that support immunity and metabolism. The result reflects both nutrition and the body response to inflammation or dehydration. It is part of standard chemistry panels.

Higher total protein can occur with dehydration or with increases in antibodies, but causes vary. Lower total protein can be seen with poor intake, absorption problems, liver issues, or kidney loss of protein, yet many day to day factors can also play a role. Exercise, posture during the draw, and body fluid shifts can nudge values slightly. Because the number combines several proteins, it does not point to one specific problem on its own. Follow up tests like albumin, globulin fractions, or urine protein may be used for a fuller picture when needed.

Aim for steady protein intake from foods such as beans, fish, eggs, tofu, dairy, nuts, and lean meats. Stay well hydrated, especially before and after strenuous activity, to avoid concentration related swings. Keep meals balanced with whole grains, fruits, and vegetables to support the liver protein production. Discuss long term restrictive diets or appetite changes with a clinician or dietitian so you can meet your needs safely. If total protein remains outside the reference range, your healthcare professional can decide whether more detailed testing makes sense.

name: Total Testosterone
description:
Testosterone is a vital male sex hormone, also present in women in smaller amounts, crucial for various bodily functions. In men, testosterone plays a key role in the development of male reproductive tissues, including the testes and prostate, and promotes secondary sexual characteristics such as increased muscle and bone mass, and the growth of body hair. It also influences libido, mood, and energy levels. In women, testosterone contributes to ovarian function, bone strength, and sexual desire.

Total testosterone represents the sum of both free testosterone and testosterone bound to proteins in the blood, such as sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. Measuring total testosterone levels provides an overall assessment of the body's testosterone production.

Low testosterone levels in men, known as hypogonadism, can lead to a range of symptoms and health issues. These can include reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased muscle mass and strength, increased body fat, decreased bone density (osteoporosis), low energy levels, fatigue, depression, and impaired cognitive function. Causes of low testosterone include aging, obesity, certain chronic diseases, and specific medical treatments. In women, low testosterone levels can result in diminished libido, fatigue, and a decrease in well-being.

Conversely, excessively high testosterone levels can cause problems as well. In men, it might be due to anabolic steroid use or testosterone supplementation, leading to aggressive behavior, acne, increased risk of heart disease, liver disease, and decreased sperm production. In women, high testosterone levels can indicate conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), manifesting in symptoms such as irregular menstrual cycles, excess hair growth, and obesity. Balancing testosterone levels through lifestyle changes, medication, or treating the underlying cause is crucial for overall health and well-being.

To maintain healthy testosterone levels:


Engage in regular exercise, particularly resistance training, as it can help boost testosterone levels naturally.
Maintain a healthy weight, as obesity can contribute to lower testosterone levels.
Ensure a balanced diet rich in protein, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates, as these nutrients are essential for hormone production and overall health.
​​​

name: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO Ab / anti-TPO / ATPO)
en_name: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO Ab / anti-TPO / ATPO)
description:
Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies are proteins made by the immune system that target the enzyme the thyroid uses to make thyroid hormones. The test shows whether these antibodies are present and, if so, at what level. Many people with autoimmune thyroid conditions have TPO antibodies, but some people with positive tests never develop thyroid problems. Values can vary over time, and different labs use different reference ranges. The result is best considered together with TSH and thyroid hormone levels and with how you feel.
Higher TPO antibody levels increase the chance of future thyroid changes, especially over the long term, but they do not predict exactly when or if symptoms will occur. Levels may rise or fall with life events such as pregnancy and the months after delivery, or with changes in iodine intake. Certain medications and supplements can interact with thyroid function, so a full medication and supplement list helps with interpretation. A positive test by itself is not a diagnosis and does not automatically require treatment. Monitoring patterns over time is a common approach when you and your clinician are watching thyroid health.
Practical steps include avoiding excess iodine from concentrated seaweed or high‑dose supplements while still meeting daily needs. Ensure adequate selenium from foods such as eggs, seafood, or a small number of Brazil nuts, unless you have been advised to avoid them. Aim for steady sleep, stress management, and a balanced diet, which support immune balance in general. If you are planning pregnancy or notice symptoms of under‑ or over‑active thyroid, arrange timely lab checks. Use this test as a guidepost and work with your clinician on a plan that fits your situation.

name: Transferrin
description:
Transferrin is the main protein that carries iron through the bloodstream to the bone marrow and other tissues. Each transferrin molecule can hold two iron atoms, which helps keep iron safe and available. The liver produces transferrin, and production adjusts based on iron status and overall health. Blood tests report transferrin concentration directly or convert it into TIBC using a factor. Together with ferritin and iron, transferrin helps describe how well your iron transport system is working.
Transferrin levels often rise when iron stores are low because the body increases its capacity to capture iron. They may fall during inflammation, chronic illness, or liver disease, which reduces production of some proteins. Pregnancy commonly increases transferrin as the body prepares for higher iron needs. Hydration, time of day, and lab methods can cause small day‑to‑day differences. No single result is diagnostic, so clinicians look at the full iron panel and your story.
Eat iron‑containing foods regularly and include vitamin C‑rich foods to help with absorption. Ensure adequate protein intake, since transferrin is a protein produced by the liver. Limit excessive tea or coffee with meals if you are working on iron absorption, as they can reduce uptake for some people. Avoid self‑prescribing high‑dose iron, which can be harmful if not needed. Recheck with the same lab after diet or treatment changes to see how transferrin responds.

name: Transferrin saturation
description:
Transferrin saturation (often called TSAT) shows what percentage of the iron-carrying protein transferrin is loaded with iron. It is calculated from two common tests, serum iron and total iron-binding capacity, and is reported as a percentage. This value gives a sense of how available iron is for making hemoglobin and supporting energy and thinking. It can vary during the day, can change after a recent meal or iron pill, and is best understood together with ferritin and a complete blood count. By itself it is a guide, not a diagnosis.
Lower TSAT usually points toward limited available iron, which can happen with low intake, heavy periods, blood donation, pregnancy, or inflammation that locks iron away. Higher TSAT can appear with too much iron from supplements or transfusions, or with certain inherited patterns where the body absorbs more iron than it needs. A recent iron tablet can temporarily spike the number without reflecting your usual status. Illness and liver conditions can also shift iron traffic and change the percentage. That is why clinicians often repeat testing and look at several iron markers together.
For steady iron balance, build meals around iron-containing foods such as legumes, lean meats, seafood, seeds, and leafy greens. Pair plant sources with vitamin C-rich foods like citrus, peppers, or tomatoes to improve absorption. Limit tea or coffee with iron-rich meals because the natural compounds in them can block absorption when taken at the same time. Only use iron supplements when recommended, because too much iron can be harmful over time. Use this percentage as an educational signal and partner with a clinician, especially if you feel tired, dizzy, or short of breath.

name: Triglycerides
description:
Triglycerides are a type of fat (lipid) found in the blood, and they serve as a major source of energy for the body. After eating, the body converts any calories it doesn't need to use right away into triglycerides, which are stored in fat cells. When the body needs energy between meals, hormones release triglycerides to fulfill the energy requirement. While triglycerides are essential for health, providing energy and serving as a source of fatty acids, their balance in the body is crucial.

High levels of triglycerides, known as hypertriglyceridemia, can contribute to the hardening and thickening of arterial walls (atherosclerosis), increasing the risk of stroke, heart attack, and heart disease. Elevated triglycerides are often a sign of other conditions that also increase the risk of heart disease and stroke, including obesity and metabolic syndrome - a cluster of conditions that includes too much fat around the waist, high blood pressure, low HDL (""good"") cholesterol, high LDL (""bad"") cholesterol, and high blood sugar. In extremely high levels, triglycerides can also lead to pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas.

Low levels of triglycerides are generally not considered a health risk. In fact, lower triglyceride levels are often seen as beneficial and are associated with a reduced risk of heart disease. However, very low levels might be a marker of other underlying conditions, such as malnutrition or malabsorption, where the body is unable to properly digest or take in nutrients from food. Maintaining a healthy balance of triglycerides is essential for overall health, and this is often achieved through diet, regular exercise, and lifestyle changes.

To maintain healthy triglyceride levels:


Adopt a diet low in simple carbohydrates, refined sugars, and saturated and trans fats. Focus on consuming complex carbohydrates, lean proteins, and healthy fats from sources like fish, nuts, and seeds.
Engage in regular physical activity, aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week.
Maintain a healthy weight, as excess body fat can contribute to elevated triglyceride levels.
If you have high triglyceride levels or are at increased risk for heart disease, work with your healthcare provider to develop a personalized management plan, which may include lifestyle changes, medication, and monitoring of other related risk factors.
​​​

name: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
description:
TSH is a hormone made by your pituitary gland (in the brain). It tells your thyroid to make thyroid hormones (T4 and T3). When T4/T3 are low, TSH usually goes up; when T4/T3 are high, TSH usually goes down. This ""feedback loop"" helps keep your body in balance. TSH affects many body systems because it controls thyroid hormone levels, which influence energy use, heart rhythm, body temperature, mood, and thinking.[Mullur, 2014]
Low TSH (often signals an overactive thyroid)
Low TSH commonly happens when the thyroid is overactive (hyperthyroidism) or when too much thyroid medicine is taken. People may notice a fast or irregular heartbeat, nervousness, heat intolerance, and weight loss. Lower TSH with higher thyroid hormone levels is linked with a higher risk of atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat).
High TSH (often signals an underactive thyroid)
High TSH usually means the thyroid is underactive (hypothyroidism). Symptoms can include tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, dry skin, and constipation. Hypothyroidism can also affect mood and thinking; treatment helps, but some symptoms may take time to improve.
To maintain healthy TSH levels

  Get enough iodine (iodized salt or foods as advised). Iodine is required to make thyroid hormones.[Zimmermann, 2009]
  Keep iron status healthy; low iron can impair thyroid hormone production.[Zimmermann & Kohrle, 2002]
  Ensure selenium intake is adequate; selenium‑dependent enzymes help activate/inactivate thyroid hormones.[Zimmermann & Kohrle, 2002]
  Tell your clinician about biotin supplements (often in ""hair/nails"" products). Biotin can distort lab results (often making TSH look falsely low). Stopping biotin before testing is often advised; follow your lab/clinician''s guidance.[Zhang, 2020]
  Some medicines (e.g., amiodarone, lithium) can affect thyroid function; monitoring may be needed.[Harjai, 1997][Lazarus, 2009]

name: Total Triiodothyronine (TT3)
description:
Total T3 measures all triiodothyronine (bound + free). T3 is the active form of the thyroid hormones, although only the free form of T3 (FT3) can enter cells and be active. TT3 can help confirm hyperthyroidism (often rises) or hypothyroidism (often falls), but it is influenced by binding proteins, so results should be read with TSH and FT4/FT3.[Garber, 2012][Koulouri, 2013]
Low TT3
Low TT3 with high TSH and low FT4 suggests hypothyroidism. Low TT3 with normal TSH in severe illness often reflects non‑thyroidal illness (the body lowers T3 during stress/illness).[Fliers, 2015]
High TT3
High TT3 with low TSH points to hyperthyroidism or over‑replacement. TT3 can also be affected by changes in binding proteins.[Koulouri, 2013]
To maintain healthy TT3 levels

  Support thyroid hormone production/activation with iodine, iron, and selenium as advised.[Zimmermann, 2009][Zimmermann & Kohrle, 2002]
  Let your clinician know about biotin and medications (e.g., amiodarone) that can shift T3 levels or distort test results.[Zhang, 2020][Ylli, 2021][Harjai, 1997]

name: Total Thyroxine (TT4)
description:
Total T4 measures all thyroxine in your blood—both bound to proteins and free. It is the storage form of the thyroid hormones (think of fuel waiting to be burned). Because most T4 is protein‑bound, TT4 is strongly affected by binding proteins (e.g., TBG). Estrogen (e.g., pregnancy, some contraceptives) raises TBG and can raise TT4 even when the thyroid is normal.[Koulouri, 2013] TT4 helps assess thyroid function, especially when interpreted alongside TSH and FT4.
Low TT4
Low TT4 with high TSH suggests hypothyroidism. Low TT4 with low/normal TSH may be central hypothyroidism or low binding proteins (e.g., low TBG) rather than true hormone shortage.[Koulouri, 2013]
High TT4
High TT4 with low TSH points to hyperthyroidism or over‑replacement. High TT4 with normal TSH may reflect higher binding proteins (e.g., pregnancy, estrogen therapy).[Koulouri, 2013]
To maintain healthy TT4 levels

  Support normal hormone production with adequate iodine and iron.[Zimmermann, 2009][Zimmermann & Kohrle, 2002]
  Maintain selenium intake for proper hormone activation.[Zimmermann & Kohrle, 2002]
  Share supplement use (biotin) and medicines (amiodarone) with your clinician, as they can change results or thyroid status.[Harjai, 1997][Lazarus, 2009][Zhang, 2020]

name: Urea (BUN)
description:
Urea, often reported as BUN (blood urea nitrogen), is a waste product made when your body breaks down protein. The liver makes urea and the kidneys filter it into urine, so the level in blood reflects protein metabolism, hydration, and kidney handling. It moves up and down with diet and fluid status more than many people realize. Because it is influenced by multiple factors, it is best used alongside creatinine and other kidney markers. Think of BUN as a snapshot of protein turnover and kidney “traffic flow.”
Higher BUN can show up with dehydration, high‑protein eating, vigorous exercise, or reduced kidney filtration. Lower BUN can appear with overhydration, pregnancy, or low protein intake, and sometimes with liver issues. Certain medications and supplements can shift BUN without reflecting a disease process. A single value is not diagnostic and should be interpreted in context, ideally with a look at trends. Testing at similar times and hydration states helps make fair comparisons.
Support balanced BUN by staying well hydrated, especially around exercise and heat. Choose protein portions that fit your size, goals, and activity level rather than pushing extremes. Emphasize vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and plant proteins alongside lean animal options if you eat them. Be cautious with pain relievers and other drugs that can stress the kidneys, using only what you need. If numbers surprise you, a repeat test after a few days of consistent fluids and routine eating often brings clarity.

name: Uric Acid
description:
Uric acid is a natural waste product formed when your body breaks down purines from cells and certain foods. Most uric acid dissolves in blood, passes through the kidneys, and leaves the body in urine. Blood levels depend on how much is made and how well it is removed. Many healthy people have stable uric acid in a wide normal range. Labs may also measure uric acid in urine to assess how much your body excretes.
Higher uric acid can be influenced by genetics, body weight, kidney function, dehydration, and diets high in purines or fructose. Alcohol, especially beer and spirits, can raise levels by increasing production and reducing excretion. Certain medicines, such as some diuretics, may nudge the value upward. Lower levels are less common and are usually not concerning by themselves. Because many factors are involved, one number is not a diagnosis and is considered together with symptoms and history.
Stay well hydrated, which helps the kidneys remove uric acid more efficiently. Limit high‑purine foods like organ meats and some fish (anchovies, sardines), and reduce sugary beverages rich in fructose. Prioritize vegetables, whole grains, low‑fat dairy, and coffee or vitamin C‑containing foods if they fit your plan. Aim for gradual, sustainable weight loss if advised, since crash diets can temporarily raise uric acid. Discuss medications and personalized targets with your clinician if your levels stay high or you have symptoms.

name: Vitamin A
description:
Vitamin A, a fat-soluble vitamin, is essential for various critical bodily functions. It is crucial for maintaining healthy vision, particularly night vision and overall eye health. Vitamin A also plays a vital role in supporting immune function, skin health, and cell growth. It exists in two primary forms: preformed vitamin A (retinol, found in animal products) and provitamin A (carotenoids, found in plant-based foods), both of which are converted to retinoic acid, the active form of the vitamin in the body. Adequate levels of vitamin A are necessary for these functions, with optimal levels varying based on age, sex, and health status.

Vitamin A deficiency can lead to several health issues, most notably affecting vision. It can cause night blindness (difficulty seeing in low light) and, in more severe cases, lead to xerophthalmia, a condition that can result in blindness. Deficiency also weakens immune function, increases susceptibility to infections, and can lead to skin issues like hyperkeratosis (thickening of the outer layer of the skin). Children and pregnant women are particularly at risk for vitamin A deficiency, which can also contribute to maternal mortality and increased susceptibility to infections like measles and diarrhea in children.

Nutrients that affect Vitamin A include fat, zinc, protein, Vitamin E, Vitamin D, and iron. Fat enhances its absorption, while zinc is crucial for its transport and metabolism. Adequate protein is important for Vitamin A transport, and Vitamin E protects it from oxidative damage. Excessive Vitamin A can interfere with Vitamin D functions and vice versa, though this is rare. Vitamin A also aids in iron metabolism, highlighting the importance of a balanced diet for effective Vitamin A utilization.

Toxicity from excessive vitamin A intake, especially from supplements, can cause hypervitaminosis A, leading to symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea, and joint pain. Chronic toxicity can result in more serious effects like liver damage, increased intracranial pressure, and birth defects if high doses are consumed during pregnancy. While toxicity from food sources is rare, it's crucial to maintain a balance, particularly with retinol forms of vitamin A. Ensuring a diet rich in a variety of sources, such as leafy green vegetables, orange and yellow vegetables, fish, and dairy products, typically provides sufficient vitamin A. Supplementation should be undertaken cautiously and under medical guidance to avoid the risk of toxicity.

To maintain healthy Vitamin A levels:
- Consume a varied diet rich in both preformed vitamin A and provitamin A sources. Include animal products like liver, fish, and dairy for retinol, and plant-based sources like sweet potatoes, carrots, and leafy greens for carotenoids.
- Ensure adequate fat intake with vitamin A-rich meals to enhance absorption, particularly when consuming plant-based sources.
- Include zinc-rich foods in your diet, such as oysters, beef, and pumpkin seeds, to support vitamin A metabolism and transport.
- Balance your intake of vitamins A, D, and E, as they work synergistically. Consider a well-balanced multivitamin if you're at risk of deficiency.​​​

name: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)
description:
Vitamin B12, or cobalamin, is crucial for red blood cell formation, nerve function, and DNA synthesis. It's vital for maintaining healthy nerve cells and the myelin sheath, and it contributes to metabolism, fatty acid synthesis, and energy production. Holotranscobalamin (holoTC), the active part of B12, indicates bioavailability for cellular use. B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia, characterized by large, immature red blood cells, leading to fatigue and weakness. It can also lead to neurological issues like numbness, confusion, and poor memory. Insufficient B12 can stem from inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption disorders, or certain medications.

B12 absorption and utilization are affected by several factors. Folate deficiency can lead to functional B12 deficiency, while high folate levels can mask B12 deficiency symptoms. The intrinsic factor, produced in the stomach, is essential for B12 absorption, and its deficiency can lead to malabsorption later on in the small intestine. Conditions affecting intrinsic factor production, such as pernicious anemia or gastric surgery, can lead to B12 malabsorption and deficiency. In such cases, alternate ways of B12 intake, such as subcutaneous injections, may be necessary to avoid deficiency. Reduced gastric acid production, as in the elderly or from certain medications, can impair B12 absorption. H. pylori infection and chronic alcohol consumption can also reduce B12 levels.

B12 toxicity is rare, as it is water-soluble, and the body typically excretes excess amounts. High B12 levels might indicate liver disease, certain leukemias, or diabetes. For most people, managing B12 involves dietary intake or supplements, particularly for vegetarians, vegans, and those at risk of deficiency. In cases of malabsorption, B12 injections or high-dose oral supplements may be necessary.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B12 levels:


Consume a balanced diet that includes B12-rich foods such as meat, fish, poultry, eggs, and dairy products. Vegetarians and vegans may need to rely on fortified foods or B12 supplements to ensure adequate intake.
If you have a malabsorption disorder or are at risk of B12 deficiency due to factors such as age, gastric surgery, or certain medications, work with your healthcare provider to determine the appropriate form and dosage of B12 supplementation.
Be aware of potential interactions with other nutrients, such as folate, which can mask B12 deficiency symptoms. Ensure adequate intake of both nutrients through a balanced diet or supplementation if necessary.
If you suspect you have a B12 deficiency or experience symptoms like fatigue, weakness, or neurological issues, consult your healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.
Avoid excessive alcohol consumption as these factors can contribute to reduced B12 levels.
​​​

name: Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) in Whole Blood
description:
Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine, is an essential nutrient that plays a crucial role in energy metabolism, particularly in the conversion of carbohydrates into glucose, which the body uses for energy. It is also vital for the proper functioning of the heart, muscles, and nervous system. Adequate levels of vitamin B1 are essential for maintaining energy levels, cognitive function, and overall cellular health. The body does not store large amounts of thiamine, so regular intake through diet or supplements is necessary. Thiamine absorption and utilization can be influenced by dietary factors: chronic alcohol consumption impairs absorption, magnesium deficiency affects its activation, and high carbohydrate diets increase thiamine demand.

Deficiency in vitamin B1 can lead to several health issues. Mild deficiency might cause symptoms like fatigue, irritability, reduced reflexes, and poor memory. Severe or prolonged deficiency can lead to beriberi, a serious condition that affects the heart and nervous system. There are two main types of beriberi: wet beriberi, which affects the cardiovascular system resulting in heart failure, and dry beriberi, affecting the nervous system leading to muscle weakness and neuropathy. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, another severe form of thiamine deficiency, is commonly associated with chronic alcoholism and can cause mental confusion, coordination problems, eye movement disturbances, and memory issues. Tannins in tea and coffee might interfere with its absorption, and sulfites in food preservatives can destroy thiamine.

Vitamin B1 toxicity is extremely rare, as it is water-soluble, and excess amounts are excreted in urine. Even at high doses, thiamine is generally considered safe. However, excessive intake through supplements might cause mild side effects like nausea or irritability. For most people, managing vitamin B1 levels involves dietary intake of thiamine-rich foods such as whole grains, meat, nuts, and legumes, or supplementation in cases of deficiency risk, like chronic alcoholism or certain medical conditions.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) levels:


Consume a balanced diet that includes thiamine-rich foods such as whole grains, lean meats, fish, nuts, legumes, and fortified foods.
Be mindful of potential interactions with dietary factors. For example, limit excessive consumption of tea and coffee, as tannins in these beverages can interfere with thiamine absorption. Also, be aware that sulfites used as food preservatives can destroy thiamine.
Ensure adequate intake of other nutrients that influence thiamine utilization, such as magnesium, through a balanced diet or supplementation if necessary.
If you suspect you have a thiamine deficiency or experience symptoms like fatigue, irritability, or poor memory, consult your healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.
​​​

name: Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)
description:
Vitamin B2, or riboflavin, helps your body turn food into energy and supports antioxidant recycling through its coenzymes FMN and FAD. It also contributes to healthy skin, eyes, and nerve function, and it is water‑soluble so the body does not store large amounts. Blood riboflavin can be measured directly or inferred from functional tests, and methods vary by laboratory. The vitamin is sensitive to light, which is why some foods and supplements are packaged in opaque containers. A measured level is informational and not a diagnosis on its own.
Lower values can reflect limited intake, poor absorption, high alcohol use, or increased needs during growth, pregnancy, or intense training. When low for a long time, people can develop symptoms such as mouth corner cracking, sore throat, or skin changes, but these signs are not specific to riboflavin alone. Higher intakes from food or supplements are generally well tolerated, and extra amounts turn urine bright yellow due to the vitamin’s natural color. Day‑to‑day variation and lab differences can nudge results without meaning a health change. Because many factors influence energy and skin health, this vitamin is considered with the rest of your nutrition and lifestyle picture.
To support steady riboflavin status, include dairy, eggs, seafood, lean meats, legumes, nuts, and green vegetables across the week. If you avoid animal foods, plan for fortified products and varied plant proteins to cover needs. Store foods and supplements away from direct light, and keep doses within evidence‑based ranges rather than megadosing. Pair nutrition with sleep and regular activity to support energy production in a balanced way. Use this marker as educational input and work with a clinician before making large supplement changes.

name: Vitamin B3 (Niacin)
description:
Vitamin B3, also called niacin, is a water‑soluble vitamin your body uses to make NAD and NADP, molecules that power hundreds of reactions. These reactions include turning food into energy, repairing DNA, and supporting normal cell signaling. Your body can obtain niacin from foods and can also make some from the amino acid tryptophan. Common food sources include meats, fish, poultry, peanuts, mushrooms, and fortified grains. Because it is water‑soluble, excess from normal foods is usually excreted rather than stored.
Low niacin intake over time can lead to symptoms of deficiency, which historically caused the condition known as pellagra. Milder shortfalls may contribute to fatigue or poor appetite, but many other factors can cause similar feelings. High supplemental doses used for lipid management can cause skin flushing, itching, stomach upset, and can stress the liver. Extended‑release products and so‑called ‘flush‑free’ forms differ in how they act and are not interchangeable. Laboratory methods vary, and a single blood level is only part of the picture when assessing nutrition.
Aim for a varied diet that includes protein foods and fortified whole grains to meet daily niacin needs. If you are considering high‑dose niacin for cholesterol, discuss risks and alternatives with a clinician first. Take niacin supplements with food to reduce flushing, and avoid alcohol at the same time, which can worsen it. Monitor liver‑related labs if you use prescription‑strength niacin under medical care. Use lab results as a guide to habits rather than a diagnosis, and recheck if you change your routine.

name: Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic Acid)
description:
Vitamin B5, also known as pantothenic acid, is essential for human health, playing a central role in energy metabolism by aiding in the breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats for energy. It is also involved in the synthesis of coenzyme A (CoA), crucial for fatty acid metabolism, and the production of red blood cells and steroid hormones. Vitamin B5 is necessary for maintaining healthy skin, hair, and eyes, and it helps in proper functioning of the nervous system and liver. As a water-soluble vitamin, it needs to be regularly consumed in the diet, as the body does not store it in large quantities.

Deficiency of vitamin B5 is extremely rare due to its widespread availability in various foods. When it does occur, it can lead to symptoms like fatigue, irritability, numbness and burning pain in the hands and feet, and sleep disturbances. Severe deficiency can result in a condition known as ""burning feet syndrome"" or acrodynia, characterized by a sensation of burning and pain in the feet. Other symptoms of deficiency may include gastrointestinal disturbances, depression, and increased susceptibility to infections due to impaired antibody production. Excessive alcohol impairs the absorption and metabolism of many nutrients, including vitamin B5, while high levels of caffeine might lead to increased excretion of the vitamin. A balanced intake of other B vitamins is also beneficial, as they work synergistically.

Toxicity from vitamin B5 is very uncommon as any excess is excreted in urine. There are no well-documented cases of harmful effects from high intake of pantothenic acid from food or supplements. However, extremely high doses might cause mild gastrointestinal distress or diarrhea. For most people, sufficient vitamin B5 intake is easily achieved through a balanced diet that includes whole grains, eggs, meat, legumes, and vegetables. Supplementation is rarely needed except in specific medical conditions, and should be undertaken under medical supervision.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B5 levels:


Consume a varied diet rich in vitamin B5 sources, including whole grains, eggs, meat, legumes, mushrooms, avocados, and broccoli.
Be mindful of factors that can affect vitamin B5 absorption and utilization, such as excessive alcohol consumption and high caffeine intake. Moderate your intake of these substances if necessary.
Ensure a balanced intake of other B vitamins, as they work synergistically with vitamin B5. Consider a B-complex supplement if you're at risk of deficiency.

name: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)
description:
Vitamin B6, also known as pyridoxine, is a crucial nutrient that plays a significant role in a wide range of bodily functions. It is essential for protein metabolism, red blood cell production, and the creation of neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine. Vitamin B6 is also involved in immune function, brain development, and maintaining normal levels of homocysteine, an amino acid in the blood. Adequate levels of vitamin B6 are necessary for optimal health, including proper nerve function and cognitive health. As a water-soluble vitamin, B6 needs to be regularly consumed in the diet, as the body does not store it in large amounts.

Deficiency in vitamin B6, though relatively rare, can lead to a range of health issues. Symptoms include anemia, skin rashes, cracked and sore lips, a swollen tongue, mood changes, weakened immune function, and in severe cases, confusion and seizures. Vitamin B6 deficiency is often associated with low levels of other B vitamins, such as B12 and folic acid, and can be caused by malabsorption syndromes, certain medications, alcoholism, or an inadequate diet. Vitamin B6's absorption and utilization are influenced by dietary protein, magnesium, and other B vitamins.

Toxicity from vitamin B6 is typically related to excessive supplementation and is rare from food sources. High doses of vitamin B6 over a prolonged period can lead to nerve damage, causing numbness and pain in the hands and feet, and in severe cases, could potentially cause neurological problems. The upper intake level for adults is set to avoid the risk of such nerve damage. To maintain adequate levels of vitamin B6, a diet including poultry, fish, potatoes, chickpeas, bananas, and fortified cereals is recommended. Regular monitoring of vitamin B6 levels is generally not necessary, except for individuals with specific medical conditions or dietary restrictions.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B6 levels:


Consume a varied diet rich in vitamin B6 sources, including poultry, fish, potatoes, non-citrus fruits, chickpeas, and fortified cereals.
Ensure adequate protein intake, as it aids in vitamin B6 absorption and utilization.[Miller, 1985]
Be aware of factors that can deplete vitamin B6, such as excessive alcohol consumption and certain medications.
Consider other nutrients that influence B6 metabolism, like magnesium and other B vitamins. A balanced diet or a B-complex supplement may be beneficial.
​​​

name: Vitamin B7 (Biotin)
description:
Biotin, also known as vitamin B7 or vitamin H, is a water-soluble B-vitamin crucial in metabolizing fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids. It is essential for the synthesis of fatty acids and in gluconeogenesis. Biotin also maintains the health of the skin, hair, and nails, influencing their strength and appearance. Biotin deficiency, though rare, can result in hair loss, skin rash, depression, lethargy, and neurological symptoms. It can be caused by inadequate dietary intake, prolonged use of anticonvulsant drugs, and genetic disorders affecting biotin metabolism.

Biotin absorption can be impacted by dietary factors and medications. Avidin, found in raw egg whites, binds to biotin and prevents its absorption; cooking neutralizes avidin. Long-term use of certain anticonvulsant medications can lower biotin levels by altering its metabolism or absorption. Chronic alcohol consumption and factors disrupting gut flora, such as prolonged antibiotic use, might affect biotin synthesis and absorption.

Biotin toxicity is virtually non-existent, with excess biotin excreted in urine. Managing biotin levels involves dietary sources like organ meats, eggs, fish, nuts, and seeds, or supplementation for those at risk of deficiency. In cases of disrupted biotin absorption, addressing the underlying causes and dietary adjustments are key for maintaining adequate levels.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B7 (Biotin) levels:


Consume a balanced diet that includes biotin-rich foods such as organ meats, eggs (cooked), fish, nuts, seeds, and certain vegetables like sweet potatoes and spinach.
If you are at risk of biotin deficiency due to factors such as prolonged antibiotic use, chronic alcohol consumption, or genetic disorders affecting biotin metabolism, consider biotin supplementation under the guidance of a healthcare professional.
If you consume raw egg whites regularly, consider reducing your intake or cooking the egg whites thoroughly, as raw egg whites contain avidin, which can interfere with biotin absorption.
​​​

name: Vitamin B9 (Folate) in Plasma
description:
Folate, also known as Vitamin B9 or folic acid in its synthetic form, is vital for DNA synthesis, repair, methylation, and red blood cell production. It's crucial for brain function and mental health, and its importance is heightened during pregnancy for fetal development, significantly reducing the risk of neural tube defects. Folate deficiency can lead to megaloblastic anemia, characterized by larger and underdeveloped red blood cells, and symptoms like fatigue and weakness. In pregnant women, low folate levels can cause birth defects, including neural tube defects.

Folate interacts with other nutrients affecting its absorption and utilization. Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to a functional folate deficiency, as B12 is necessary to recycle folate in the body. Conversely, high folate levels can mask B12 deficiency symptoms. Zinc deficiency can impair folate utilization, while chronic alcohol consumption can reduce folate absorption and increase its excretion. Certain medications, like antiepileptic drugs, can interfere with folate absorption and metabolism.

Folate toxicity is rare due to its water-soluble nature, with excess typically excreted in urine. However, excessive folic acid intake can mask vitamin B12 deficiency symptoms without preventing neurological damage caused by the deficiency.

To maintain healthy Vitamin B9 (folate) levels:


Consume a varied diet rich in folate-containing foods, such as leafy green vegetables, citrus fruits, legumes, whole grains, and fortified foods.
If you have a genetic variant affecting folate metabolism (such as MTHFR), work with your healthcare provider to determine the appropriate form and dosage of folate supplementation.
Be mindful of potential interactions with medications, such as antiepileptic drugs, that can interfere with folate absorption and metabolism. Discuss any concerns with your healthcare provider.
Ensure adequate intake of other nutrients that influence folate utilization, such as vitamin B12 and zinc, through a balanced diet or supplementation if necessary.
